text: The key to great trading: stop judging yourself and stop forecasting. When conditions are bullish, act bullish; when they’re bearish, adjust. Trust your process. You’ll buy stocks that go to zero and sell some that go to infinity—the key is what you do in between. You will make many mistakes; you’ll never trade perfectly. You can only learn to perfectly trade your plan. Making mistakes is trading. Mitigating them is professional trading.

When I look at the legends — or better yet, the ones I aspire to stand alongside — I’m not talking about people who “made six figures trading.” I’m looking at traders who turned swing trading and market timing into eight-, nine-, even ten-figure empires and built an extraordinary life around it.

It wasn’t just trading or investing per se that got them there — it was aspiration, desire, process and grit.

So let me call them out by name...

1.) Paul Tudor Jones is sitting around $7.5 billion, one of the most successful macro swing traders to ever do it.

2.) Stanley Druckenmiller, roughly $6.2 billion, put up an almost comically good track record with no losing years for decades.

3.) Steve Cohen, at about $19 billion, isn’t a pure swing trader, but his desk built and ran the greatest short-term trading engine Wall Street has ever seen.

4.) Jesse Livermore, at his peak, sat on the equivalent of $1.5 billion in today’s dollars — he built and lost multiple fortunes, but the peak was enormous.

5.) @DanZanger turned $10,000 into $42 million in 23 months, probably the most explosive retail run on record.

6.) @markminervini , a multiple-time U.S. Investing Champion, is comfortably in the 8–9 figure camp.

7.) William O’Neil, founder of Investor’s Business Daily and the CAN SLIM framework, stacked up hundreds of millions.

8.) Nicolas Darvas took $25,000 to $2.25 million in the 1960s — over $20 million in today’s terms.

9.) Linda Raschke @ra97042_linda has been one of the most consistently profitable traders of the modern era, with a long-term net worth well into the seven- or eight-figure range.

Most investors are too busy—and too worried about missing the next big winner—that they pay far less attention to the far greater danger: losing money and holding big losers. That fear of missing out leads them into the inevitability of regression, volatility, and eventually deep drawdowns.
What they don’t realize is that hindsight is a magician. If you Monday-morning quarterback your trades, you will always find stocks that went much higher after you sold them. But that’s an illusion. The only thing that’s real is the present moment, and risk can only be managed in real time—never in retrospect.
There’s a fortune embedded in this message. Unfortunately, only a few truly understand its meaning… and even fewer appreciate its value.
